title: Amortized Analysis
summary: A rare expensive operation doesn't ruin the average cost per call if it's spread across enough cheap ones — the dynamic array's doubling resize is the canonical proof, and the technique behind why push_back is 'O(1)' at all.

slides.markdown:
Every time you're told `list.append()` or `ArrayList.add()` is O(1), that's a small lie of convenience. Occasionally, that call has to grow the backing array — copy every existing element into a bigger block — which is an O(n) operation, not O(1).

**Amortized analysis** is the technique that makes the O(1) claim honest anyway: instead of asking "what does the worst single call cost," it asks "what does a call cost *on average*, over a long sequence, in the worst case sequence of calls." One O(n) resize, spread across the n cheap pushes that made it necessary, averages out to O(1) per push.

This matters beyond dynamic arrays: it's the same reasoning behind why hash table resizing doesn't ruin O(1) average insert, why a stack-based algorithm using push/pop can still be O(n) total despite individual pops sometimes doing more work, and it's a real interview question on its own — "is this O(1)?" often has an amortized answer, not a worst-case one.

A dynamic array (`list`, `ArrayList`, `vector`) keeps a backing array with **capacity** ≥ its current **length**. When a push arrives and length equals capacity, there's no room — the array allocates a **new backing block, double the old capacity**, copies every existing element across, then appends the new one.

That resize is O(n): copying n elements takes n operations. But it doesn't happen on every push — it happens only when the array is completely full, which (starting from empty) occurs at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, … — capacities that themselves double.

The key design choice is doubling the capacity rather than growing it by a fixed amount, and the next slide is entirely about why that choice is what makes the whole scheme work.

slides.sectionTitle: Why doubling, not a fixed increment
slides.markdown:
Suppose instead the array grew capacity by a **fixed amount** — say +10 — every time it filled up. Starting from empty and pushing n elements, a resize happens every 10 pushes: n/10 resizes total, each copying a multiple of 10 elements (10, 20, 30, … up to n). That total copy work is **1+2+...+(n/10)** in units of 10, which sums to **O(n²)** — the fixed-growth scheme is quadratic overall, O(n) per push on average, not O(1).

Doubling avoids this because resizes get **exponentially rarer** relative to their size. Resizes happen at 1, 2, 4, 8, …, 2^k elements — only **log n** resizes total for n pushes — and even though each one is more expensive than the last, the *total* copy work across all of them is bounded by a geometric series: 1+2+4+...+n ≈ **2n**, still O(n) — linear, not quadratic, spread across n pushes.

That's the entire trick: doubling makes the total resize cost proportional to the final size, not to the number of resizes times their sizes.

slides.sectionTitle: Charging the resize to the pushes that earned it
slides.markdown:
A useful mental model (the **accounting method**): imagine every push pays a small constant surcharge into a savings account, on top of its own O(1) work. By the time the array fills up and a resize is due, the accumulated savings from all the pushes since the last resize are exactly enough to pay for copying them.

Concretely: charge each push 3 "credits" instead of 1. One credit pays for the push itself; the other two go to savings. When the array resizes at size 2k, the k pushes since the last resize (at size k) have banked 2k credits — exactly enough to pay for copying k old elements plus setting aside credit for the *next* resize's first half. The resize looks free from the outside because it was pre-paid by the operations that made it necessary.

slides.subTitle: Total cost over m operations, divided by m
slides.markdown:
The **aggregate method** is the simplest way to compute an amortized bound: run the whole sequence of m operations, sum the *total* cost across all of them, then divide by m. Whatever comes out is the amortized cost per operation — no per-operation accounting needed.

For n pushes into an initially empty dynamic array: the n pushes themselves cost O(1) each, so O(n) total. The resizes happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, …, up to n, copying a total of roughly 1+2+4+...+n ≈ 2n elements — also O(n) total. Grand total: **O(n) + O(n) = O(n)** for n pushes, so the amortized cost **per push is O(n)/n = O(1)**.

This is the fastest way to get the headline number ("amortized O(1)"), though it doesn't tell you *which* individual operations are expensive — for that, the accounting method's per-operation credit story, or the more general potential-function method, is more informative.

slides.sectionTitle: Simulating the doubling and counting copies
slides.markdown:
```python
def simulate_pushes(n):
    capacity = 1
    length = 0
    total_copies = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        if length == capacity:
            capacity *= 2
            total_copies += length   # copy every existing element
        length += 1
    return total_copies

# simulate_pushes(16) -> total_copies = 15
# 15 total copies spread across 16 pushes: ~1 copy per push on average
```

Running this for n = 16 gives 15 total copy operations (1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15) across 16 pushes — under one copy per push on average, confirming the O(n) total / O(1) amortized claim empirically, not just algebraically. Try n = 1,000,000 and the ratio holds just as well: total copies stay just under n, however large n gets.

| Guarantee | What it promises | Dynamic array push |
|---|---|---|
| **Worst-case O(1)** | Every single call, individually, costs O(1) | False — a resizing push costs O(n) |
| **Amortized O(1)** | Any sequence of m calls costs O(m) total, so the average is O(1) | True — this is the actual guarantee |

The two are not interchangeable, and the difference matters operationally: a system with a **hard per-call latency budget** (a real-time audio pipeline, a control loop) can be broken by an amortized guarantee, because nothing stops the one expensive resize from landing exactly on the call that had no slack. A system that only cares about **total throughput** over many calls is fine with amortized — the occasional spike washes out.

This is precisely why some real-time systems pre-allocate capacity up front and never let a dynamic array resize during the hot path — they need the worst-case guarantee, and amortized O(1) doesn't provide it.

A common misreading: hearing "amortized O(1)" and assuming every call in practice runs fast. It doesn't — it means the **average across the whole sequence** is O(1); any single call can still be the expensive one.

Concretely, if you're pushing into a dynamic array and profiling latency per call, you will see a spike exactly at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, … — the resize points — even though the amortized claim over the full run is completely correct. If you only look at one call in isolation and it happens to be a resize, "O(1)" will look false; the guarantee is about the *sequence*, not any individual member of it.

This is why amortized analysis is sometimes the wrong tool to reach for when a candidate asks "can you guarantee that?" (see `best-worst-average-case`) — an amortized bound is not a per-call guarantee, and conflating the two is a specific, nameable mistake worth avoiding out loud in an interview: "amortized O(1), but any single push could be the O(n) resize."

slides.sectionTitle: Where else amortized analysis shows up
slides.markdown:
Dynamic array doubling is the canonical example, but the same reasoning applies anywhere a rare expensive step is funded by many cheap ones:

- **Hash table resizing** (see `hash-table-mechanics`) doubles its bucket array the same way, for the same reason — amortized O(1) insert despite occasional O(n) rehashes.
- **A stack used to process n items where each item can be pushed once and popped at most once** — even if a single operation looks like it could loop, the *total* pushes plus pops across the whole run is bounded by 2n, so the whole algorithm is O(n), not O(n²), even though a naive per-call view might suggest otherwise.
- **Splay trees and self-adjusting data structures** guarantee amortized O(log n) per operation, not worst-case, by letting some operations restructure the tree more than others in a way that pays off later.

The pattern to recognize: whenever you see "each element can only be touched a constant number of times across the whole run," that's usually an amortized-O(1)-per-operation argument in disguise, and it's worth naming explicitly rather than trying to bound a single call's cost in isolation.

A complete amortized answer names three things: **the bound** ("amortized O(1) per push"), **the mechanism** ("because doubling capacity means resize cost forms a geometric series that sums to O(n) total, not the O(n²) a fixed increment would give"), and **the caveat** ("but any single push can still be the O(n) resize — if you need a hard per-call bound, pre-allocate").

That third part is the one most candidates skip, and it's the one that reads as senior: knowing the average is good is not the same as knowing when the average isn't the guarantee you actually need. The next topic extends this same "what actually counts" scrutiny to space rather than time — specifically, why the recursive call stack is memory too, and why it's easy to undercount.
